source.title: LoRA-MGPO: Mitigating Double Descent in Low-Rank Adaptation via Momentum-Guided Perturbation Optimization
source.authors: Yu-Peng Chang; Chen-Lu Guo; Yi Chang; Yuan Wu

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendix; no apparent truncation affecting the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: Reports LoRA training-loss instability as rank increases and evaluates a mitigation in large language model fine-tuning, a new setting for the cataloged generalization claims.
record.gate_note: The paper measures training-loss trajectories and benchmark performance, but does not measure the training–test error gap, fit random labels, or report test error across a capacity sweep. Its benchmark comparisons are outcomes for its proposed optimizer and baselines; only the described loss-trajectory results directly concern the instability it targets.
record.test_reason: The study uses flat-minimum optimization as motivation for a new LoRA method and reports training stability and benchmark performance. None of its results tests V1–V8. Its double descent is a rebound in training loss over steps, rather than V2's held-out error across widths beyond interpolation. It neither measures magnitude-aware sharpness nor relates it to generalization gaps as V7 requires.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: LoRA-MGPO reduces training instability and improves benchmark performance over standard LoRA and the tested PEFT baselines. Their double descent terminology refers to transient training-loss divergence. They interpret the improvements as better generalization through flatter minima, but do not directly measure sharpness or its relationship to generalization gaps.
record.recipe_differences: Applies momentum-guided perturbation and adaptive perturbation normalization during LoRA fine-tuning; experiments use language models and report loss trajectories and downstream benchmark scores, not the original random-label/generalization-gap tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-loss behavior varies with LoRA rank and learning rate; the authors report increasingly severe standard-LoRA double descent as rank rises and oscillations at higher learning rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard LoRA exhibits a training-loss rebound that becomes more severe at higher ranks and oscillations at higher learning rates; LoRA-MGPO is reported to maintain smoother convergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Momentum-guided perturbation with adaptive normalization stabilizes LLaMA-2-7B LoRA fine-tuning on MetaMathQA across the tested ranks and learning rates.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The relevant rank and learning-rate trajectory results are presented in figures without numerical values. The paper does not report a training–test error gap for these analyses.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream benchmark tables compare LoRA-MGPO and other PEFT methods, but do not measure the training–test gap or a claim-version behavior; omitted. Figure 1 is introductory motivation and not a reported experiment in the results section.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Held-out error across network widths beyond the width needed for zero training error. Table 2's adapter-rank comparisons establish neither this threshold nor a network-width sweep.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; all experiments use AdamW.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove those effects.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurements, their association with training–test gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; the qualitative training-stability findings themselves are explicitly reported. Benchmark tables and ablations are already declared in rows_left_out and supply no missing tests of these versions.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label test accuracy.
LoRA rank is varied, but the paper does not test networks past a zero-training-error width threshold or measure test error across that threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measure or comparison of generalization gaps.

rows.subject: LoRA
rows.operation_detail: Compared training-loss trajectories across LoRA ranks.
rows.measure: Training loss trajectory; authors report a sharp rebound at rank 128.
rows.baseline: LoRA at lower ranks; exact values not stated.
rows.value: Sharp rebound at r = 128; figure values not stated.
rows.note: The text describes the result; precise plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The rank-128 training-loss rebound is explicitly reported in Section 3.3, but cannot establish any claim version. LoRA rank and training-loss trajectories do not measure V2's width-dependent test error beyond zero training error.

rows.operation_detail: Compared training-loss trajectories across LoRA ranks.
rows.measure: Training loss trajectory; authors report smooth, monotonically decreasing loss across all tested ranks.
rows.baseline: LoRA at corresponding ranks; exact values not stated.
rows.value: Smooth and monotonically decreasing across all ranks; figure values not stated.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the ranks tested; not a test-error or generalization-gap measure.
